det_01.label: Origin: Kucharski's CAPphrase quiz
det_01.content: The dataset comes from an online quiz titled 'How likely is ‘likely’?' created as an independent side project by epidemiologist and mathematician Adam Kucharski (London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine). Participants did two tasks: (1) they typed a numeric value from 0–100% for each of 19 common probability phrases (the 'absolute judgements'), and (2) they were shown pairs of phrases and asked which conveyed a higher probability (the 'pairwise comparisons'), seeing 10 pairs each — 9 unique plus 1 repeated pair as an internal consistency check. The released CAPphrase dataset (Comparative and Absolute Probability phrase) contains responses from 5,174 participants and over 150,000 individual language judgements, and is open-access with a DOI (10.5281/zenodo.18750055). It was featured as the TidyTuesday dataset for 2026-03-10, curated by Nicola Rennie.

det_02.label: Sherman Kent and the 'serious possibility' problem
det_02.content: The core problem this dataset probes is decades old. In 1951 a US National Intelligence Estimate said there was a 'serious possibility' of a Soviet attack on Yugoslavia. When CIA analyst Sherman Kent — later called the 'father of intelligence analysis' — polled colleagues on what 'serious possibility' meant numerically, answers ranged from a 20% chance to an 80% chance for the very same phrase. Kent's 1964 essay 'Words of Estimative Probability' argued that verbal probability terms are dangerously ambiguous and proposed a fixed scale mapping words to numbers (e.g. 'probable' = 75% ±12%, 'almost certain' = 93% ±6%, 'chances about even' = 50%). The Kucharski quiz is essentially a crowd-sourced, 5,000-person rerun of Kent's experiment.

det_03.label: Official scales: Kent, NIC, IPCC
det_03.content: Several institutions have tried to standardise probability words. Kent's CIA scale: certain 100%, almost certain ~93%, probable ~75%, chances about even ~50%, probably not ~30%, almost certainly not ~7%, impossible 0%. The IPCC climate scale: 'virtually certain' >99%, 'very likely' >90%, 'likely' >66%, 'about as likely as not' 33–66%, 'unlikely' <33%, 'very unlikely' <10%. UK intelligence (the Professional Head of Intelligence Assessment 'probability yardstick') officially defines 'realistic possibility' as 40–50%. These provide external benchmarks against which the crowd's interpretations can be measured — and against which disagreement can be quantified.

det_04.label: Kucharski's own headline findings
det_04.content: In his write-up, Kucharski reported several patterns the analysis should check against. 'Realistic possibility' showed the most variance — it 'meant a lot of different things to different people' despite the UK's official 40–50% definition. Respondents almost unanimously agreed 'almost no chance' is lower than 'will happen', but split nearly 50/50 on whether 'could happen' or 'might happen' is higher. People love round numbers: more than half of all absolute estimates were multiples of 10, nearly a third ended in 5, and about one in five participants rounded every single estimate. Demographic effects were real but small: Americans gave estimates ~1.03x higher than British respondents, age effects were minimal (55–64 gave ~0.97x vs the 35–44 reference). Kucharski himself questioned whether 1–3% differences, though statistically significant in such a large sample, matter in practice.

det_05.label: Why it matters: real-world stakes of vague words
det_05.content: Estimative phrases are not academic. They appear in intelligence assessments that inform war decisions, in IPCC climate reports read by policymakers, in medical consent conversations ('this side effect is common'), in legal standards ('reasonable doubt'), in weather forecasts, and in financial disclosures. When 'likely' can mean 55% to one reader and 90% to another, the same sentence can justify opposite decisions. The 1986 Challenger disaster and various intelligence failures have been linked in part to miscommunicated uncertainty. The dataset's value is that it measures, at population scale, exactly how much ambiguity these everyday words carry — and which ones are most treacherous.

det_06.label: Related work: replicated academic findings
det_06.content: Kucharski's crowd quiz sits in a long line of formal studies. A NATO study asked 23 officers (squadron leader to lieutenant general) to put numbers on probability words and found they did NOT use the Sherman Kent scale even when familiar with it. Academic work (e.g. the University of Illinois 'Perception of Probability Words' visualization, and survey studies) consistently finds wide between-person variance for mid-range terms and tighter agreement at the extremes ('certain', 'impossible'). This means the analyst's findings — if disagreement is largest in the middle and smallest at the ends — would confirm a robust, repeatedly observed pattern rather than a quirk of this one sample.

det_07.label: Scope suggestion for the Analyst
det_07.content: Focus the analysis on: (1) per-phrase distributions — mean, median, and especially SPREAD (std dev / IQR) to find which phrases provoke most disagreement; compare the most-disagreed phrase to the UK's 40–50% definition of 'realistic possibility'. (2) Internal consistency between the two tasks — does the rank order from absolute values match who-beats-whom in pairwise comparisons? Look for phrases that flip (a phrase rated higher on average but that loses head-to-head). (3) Round-number bias — quantify the multiples-of-10 and ending-in-5 effect and the share of respondents who rounded everything. (4) Order effects — does the 'order' column correlate with the value given (anchoring)? (5) Demographics — compute an 'optimism' index per country / age / English-background / education, but flag that effects are likely small (1–3%). Caveat throughout: this is a self-selected online sample, not representative; do not claim causation.

reference_media.description: The author's own ranked dot-plot: each of the 19 phrases on the y-axis, every individual response as a dot on the 0–100% x-axis, with mean (hollow red circle) and median (red diamond). 'Will Happen' tops it (median 100%, mean 98%); 'Almost No Chance' is bottom (median 2%). Several mid phrases ('Realistic Possibility', 'May/Might/Could Happen') span nearly the full 0–100% range — the visual proof of the disagreement story.
